faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Darlington?
faqs.a: It depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing and cleanup the home needs afterward. Our crew inspects first, shows you the entry points we found, and gives you a quote after inspection before any removal or sealing work begins — no prices are promised over the phone.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Darlington home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

The homes here sit in Pee Dee farm and mill-town land along Black Creek, with river swamp on the eastern edge, and that habitat explains most of what we find: raccoons, gray squirrels, opossums, armadillos account for the bulk of our Darlington calls, moving between the wild ground and the housing along the same creeks, field edges, and canopy streets every night.

Mill-era and farm-town homes with porches and crawlspaces, plus newer subdivisions on flat sandy lots around Hartsville. In spring we handle denning raccoons and squirrels before litters grow, in summer the calls shift to bats, skunks, and digging animals in the yards, and in fall we seal homes ahead of the winter push. Every Darlington job starts with a full inspection of the roofline, foundation, and crawlspace, and ends with the entries sealed — because in Darlington County there is always another animal nearby ready to use an open hole.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Hartsville home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Most snakes our crew is called about here are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide, and — only in the wet coastal and swamp country — the cottonmouth. We identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, and tell us where it went. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is never handled as a removal job, and venomous snakes are safety-and-referral work, not a guaranteed capture.

faqs.q: There is a dead animal smell in my Hartsville walls. What should I do?
faqs.a: Call us rather than opening walls at random. Our crew locates the carcass — a dead raccoon, opossum, or squirrel in a wall void or crawlspace is the usual source — removes it, and sanitizes the area. Carcasses of raccoons, skunks, and bats are handled with rabies precautions in line with Department of Public Health guidance, and we check how the animal got in so the entry is sealed as part of the same visit.

faqs.q: An opossum keeps getting under my Lamar house. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Opossums den under houses because crawlspaces near farm roads and creek bottoms south of Darlington are dry, dark, and close to pet food and trash. One opossum is mostly a nuisance; a season of them brings droppings, torn insulation, and fleas. We trap the animal — opossums are handled under depredation rules, since routine relocation is not permitted in South Carolina — then screen vents and repair the crawlspace door so the shelter is gone, not just the tenant.

faqs.q: Pigeons and starlings are nesting in my Lamar vents. Can they be removed?
faqs.a: Pigeons, European starlings, and house sparrows are the birds we can work on in Lamar — vents screened, nests cleared, and spikes or netting fitted so the birds move on. Native birds are different: woodpeckers, chimney swifts, and nesting songbirds are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, so those jobs are deterrence and timing, waiting out the nest and sealing after the young fledge. Around farm roads and creek bottoms south of Darlington, vent and soffit nests are the calls we see most.

faqs.q: How do you price the work on a Lamar home?
faqs.a: Honestly, it depends on what the inspection turns up — and in Lamar that is rarely just one hole. Attic contamination, the number of openings to seal in steel, crawlspace repairs, and whether the job needs return visits for trapping all shape the work. We itemize what we find, explain which items stop the problem for good and which are optional, and let you decide with the full list in hand.

Lamar.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Lamar and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the farm roads and creek bottoms south of Darlington. Homeowners here phone us first about armadillos in sandy field-edge yards, then about bats in tobacco-barn and gable roosts.

Housing here runs from historic in-town streets to farm roads, and most of it predates modern sealed construction — open vents and pier foundations are the norm. Blackwater rivers and swamp drains thread this farm country, and wildlife follows them: raccoons, opossums, and armadillos work the wet edges, then den in the nearest barn, porch, or crawlspace.

Before we leave a Lamar home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

Society Hill.wildlife_intro:
The pattern in Society Hill is set by the Great Pee Dee River bluff and historic Welsh Neck settlement. If we had to name this town's signature jobs, they would be raccoons following swamp drains and striped skunks under porches.

Farmhouses, older in-town homes, and small subdivisions on flat ground make up the stock, with barns, sheds, and grain storage close enough to houses to share the same wildlife. Tobacco barns, grain storage, and older farmhouses give Pee Dee wildlife food and shelter in the same footprint, so jobs here often pair structure exclusion with yard and outbuilding work.

Every job in Society Hill ends the same way it should: openings found on the inspection closed in steel mesh and flashing, so the house near Great Pee Dee River bluff and historic Welsh Neck settlement stops advertising vacancies to the next animal that passes.
